sentences.text: Saltasaurus holds the distinction of being the first sauropod genus discovered to possess armor made of bony plates embedded directly in its skin.
Hundreds of females are known to have dug holes with their hind legs to create nesting sites.
The small eggs, measuring roughly 11 to 12 centimeters across, contained embryos with skin impressions revealing a mosaic of tiny bead-like scales.
Excavations led by José Bonaparte, Martín Vince, and Juan C. Leal took place between 1975 and 1977 at the Estancia El Brete.
The initial find consisted of a group of six incomplete skeletons.
These fossils were located within the Balbuena subgroup of the Salta Group inside the El Brete Formation.
Bonaparte and Jaime E. Powell formally named and described the species in 1980.
Like all members of the sauropod group, this animal was a herbivore.
Its diet consisted entirely of plant material.
The creature was graviportal, a term describing sauropods whose hind legs remained straight during the loading phase of walking, preventing them from running.
Earlier theories suggested that sheer size was enough to deter predators from attacking these massive reptiles.
Powell proposed that adults relied on their body armor for protection, whereas young individuals depended on the safety of the herd.
This assumption distinguished the defensive strategies of mature individuals from those of the juvenile population.
Powell also suggested that the animal lived in an aquatic environment.
The genus belongs to the family Saltasauridae, a group previously known as Titanosauridae before being redefined with Saltasaurus as the type genus.
Loricosaurus scutatus is considered a possible synonym for Saltasaurus.
Armor plates once named Loricosaurus by Friedrich von Huene are now thought to belong to Saltasaurus rather than to ankylosaurians.
Although relationships within Titanosauria remain highly controversial, most studies agree that Saltasaurus is one of the most derived titanosaur genera.
This animal lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately between 73 and 66 million years ago, in what is now South America.
Its time range corresponds to the Maastrichtian stage, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
Saltasaurus was one of the titanosaurid sauropods that lived about 70 million years ago.

The discovery proved that titanosaurs were the dominant fauna in South America during the Late Cretaceous, contradicting the view that hadrosaurs like Edmontosaurus displaced primitive sauropods globally as they did in Laurasia.

Since bony armor was previously known only in thyreophorans, Saltasaurus demonstrated that massive sauropods did not need additional protection, helping to reclassify armored finds like Titanosaurus from nodosaurids.
Since then, paleontologists have investigated the possibility that other sauropods also had armor, such as Laplatasaurus.
